prize_parts.citation: For their theory of strategic bargaining, from the alternating-offers model of bilateral negotiation to its extension to bargaining in decentralised markets.

statement.case_for: My configuration has changed. I now put B001 first, with Rubinstein and Wolinsky, and move B030 to an alternative. In round 1 my main reservation about B001 was prior recognition of game theory. Andersson's reply answers it. The earlier awards covered equilibrium and refinement, incomplete information and mechanism design. Rubinstein's 1982 model is a positive account of how negotiation unfolds, with a unique subgame-perfect outcome that links patience to bargaining power. It is a different object from those awards. The Rubinstein-Wolinsky market-bargaining work carries that logic into decentralised price formation, which is the part of the result I know best from industrial organisation. There, bargaining protocols now sit under models of supplier-retailer negotiation, wage setting and search-based price formation. The result is about forty years old and its validity is uncontested. The credit is also cleaner than in most candidates: Rubinstein for the core model and Wolinsky for the market extension. I do not base the move on the count of colleagues who ranked B001. I base it on Andersson's argument about what the prior prizes did and did not cover, and on my reassessment of my own first choice. B030 is a strong methods contribution, but its attribution is unsettled, its dynamic branch is unevenly adopted, and my enthusiasm for it may partly reflect familiarity with the field. For a final public configuration I want the achievement with the clearest conceptual content and the least dispute over who did it.
statement.case_against: The prior-prize concern is reduced, not removed. The Committee has honoured game theory several times, and a reader could see a bargaining award as more of the same tradition. The direct empirical test of the alternating-offers model is limited, and it informs applied work mainly through structure and intuition, not through estimated quantities. Teorell and Strömberg make this point, and I take it as a real discount relative to B002 and B038, whose evidence can be examined against data. The credit boundaries are not fully closed. Binmore's Nash-programme work and Ståhl's earlier finite-horizon results (a Swedish precursor that I am glad to see raised openly) complicate the lineage. Wolinsky's share rests on one market-bargaining extension. A committee that weights demonstrated empirical influence and recent policy reach could fairly prefer another candidate.

responses.point: Andersson ranks B001 first and replied to my B030 case. He argues that earlier game-theory prizes covered equilibrium theory, incomplete information and mechanism design, and that Rubinstein's positive model of negotiation is a distinct branch. He also agrees that Binmore is the weaker claim and accepts that the BLP attribution is clean.
responses.response: This reply moved me, and it is the main reason my configuration changed. My round-1 objection treated bargaining as part of an already-honoured field. His distinction is a fair reading of what those awards were about. On B030 I still hold that structural demand estimation is a substantive way of learning about competition from data. I accept his view that it is a methods contribution with mixed uptake in its dynamic branch. I also accept that the omission of Bresnahan and Reiss under a three-name cap is a cost I should not wave away. On credit we agree: the prize should go to Rubinstein and Wolinsky, with Binmore left out. I would add that the citation should name the alternating-offers model and the market extension and should not claim the whole Nash programme.

responses.point: Teorell accepts the scientific standing of B001 but says maturity alone does not separate candidates whose validity is uncontested. He weights work whose measurement and causal content can be checked against data, and he wants Binmore's place settled before any B001 configuration is final.
responses.response: I agree that maturity alone does not decide the choice, and I do not rest on it. My case is that the result gave economists a new object: a tractable, testable account of how patience and outside options determine the split. The market version ties it to price formation, which is empirically relevant in IO and labour. I do accept that its empirical bite is indirect, and I count that against B001 relative to B002. I would also settle Binmore now, not leave it open. His Nash-programme work and experimental interests are real, but the core model and the market extension are Rubinstein's and Wolinsky's. A two-name citation is defensible on that basis. If the Committee wants a Binmore claim carried, I would see that as a reason to narrow the citation, not to add a third name.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B041 first, with Melitz as originator and Helpman as co-recipient. He names Melitz alone as his fallback and lists B001 as an alternative. In answering my round-1 point he acknowledged that the credit of Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum cannot be honoured within the ballot.
responses.response: His acknowledgement is the issue I raised in round 1, and it is why I now put B041 below B001. The mechanism is a real contribution. The ballot cannot fairly credit the parallel claims of Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, and the welfare gains from selection depend on specification. Helpman's presence on both B013 and B041 adds a framing problem that B001 does not have. I do not think this lowers B041 much on scientific merit, and I would support Melitz alone as a coherent fallback if the Committee prefers trade. I am wary of my own pull toward it, because I work in this field. B001's attribution is simply less contested. Since he lists B001 as an alternative, I hope he will weigh it on those terms.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B038 first and replied to my seventh-place ranking. She argues that the shift-share criticism concerns inference and exposure design, that the core finding of large and persistent local adjustment costs has survived reanalysis, and that a contribution which has survived its own scrutiny scores well on maturity.
responses.response: I accept part of this. The criticism has refined the conditions for valid identification and has not overturned the qualitative finding, and I now rate B038 higher than my seventh place. It is a serious alternative, and a citation limited to the China-shock evidence and local labour-market adjustment would answer most of my attribution worry. I still place it second to B001 for this stage, for two reasons. The magnitude and persistence of the effects are still contested, which matters for a prize built on empirical findings. The prize rationale also remains harder to state because of the task-framework lineage, which Enflo and Fredriksson also say they do not want to claim. If the Committee settles on B038, I could support Autor, Dorn and Hanson on that narrow citation. I do not agree that B038 is clearly more mature than B001. A theory with forty years of use is not less mature than an empirical agenda with fifteen.

responses.point: Strömberg ranks B001 eighth. He accepts that the alternating-offers model is canonical but sees a weaker link to observed contracts and policy than for his preferred programmes, and he notes that game theory is well covered by earlier prizes. He also calls the Wolinsky, Binmore and Ståhl attribution questions less settled than a Grossman-Helpman pair.
responses.response: The weaker link to observed contracts is the strongest reservation against B001, and I count it. I would qualify it in one respect. Bargaining protocols are now used in applied work on negotiated prices, for example supplier-retailer negotiations. They are also used in search-based models of wages and prices, so the link exists, though it comes through structure and not through direct tests. I disagree that attribution is less settled than for Grossman-Helpman. Rubinstein is the clear originator, Wolinsky has a distinct and well-known extension, and Binmore and Ståhl are best treated as lineage or secondary contributions. I do not claim that is certain. I rely on general knowledge here and have not independently verified the literature. His point about prior prizes is the one I weighed longest, and Andersson's reply answers it for me.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee treats earlier game-theory prizes as bearing on a bargaining award, or as covering a different branch. This is the main reason I could be wrong about ranking B001 first.

Whether the right laureate set is Rubinstein and Wolinsky, Rubinstein alone, or a set that gives a place to Binmore or recognises Ståhl's finite-horizon precursor. I currently judge two names to be the most defensible.

How much weight a conceptual theory prize with indirect empirical content should carry against empirical programmes with documented influence (B038, B002), without field familiarity deciding the comparison.
My move away from B030 may itself reflect a wish to appear less partial toward my own field. I have tried to base it on the attribution and uptake arguments above, but I cannot rule that out.

If B001 does not advance, my fallbacks are B030 with Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes on a demand-estimation citation, and B041 with Melitz alone or with Helpman. I could also support B038 on a narrow China-shock citation. These are fallbacks, not a view that any of them is stronger on the merits.
My assessments rely on the supplied evidence and general knowledge, without independent verification of the literature.
statement.conflict_note: No change in substance. No recusal-level connection is apparent from the supplied profile. None of Rubinstein, Wolinsky or Binmore is among my listed co-authors (Asplund, Steen, Ulsaker, Grönqvist, Wilander, Syverson, Goldstein), and none of the credited names on B030, B041 or B038 is either. I work in industrial organisation and international trade, which is adjacent to B030 and B041, and bargaining models are also used in IO. I treat that familiarity as a disclosure, not as evidence of merit, and I note that my preferred part has moved away from my closest field. I co-authored a 2026 paper with the chair, John Hassler, and with former chair Tore Ellingsen, which is not a connection to any candidate. Andersson, Dreber, Strömberg and I share an SSE affiliation, which is a colleague connection and not a candidate connection. My spouse's public political role (Magdalena Andersson) is noted as a public fact only, and I see no bearing on any shortlisted candidate.
